column1: In the hardware matching exercise, which component is the "brain of the computer"?
column2: The CPU.

column1: Which hardware component provides short-term, quick data storage?
column2: Memory (RAM).

column1: Which hardware component provides long-term, safe data storage?
column2: Storage, e.g. a Solid State Drive (SSD).

column1: What is the role of the network in the hardware matching exercise?
column2: The connection between computers.

column1: What is a GPU described as?
column2: A massively parallel processor for computations.

column1: How many bytes per second can a 2.5 GHz 64-bit CPU process (lecture estimate)?
column2: $2.5 \times 10^9 \times 8 = 20 \times 10^9$ bytes per second, assuming one 8-byte operation per cycle.

column1: How many bytes can 16 GB of RAM and a 1 TB SSD store?
column2: $16 \times 10^9$ bytes and $1 \times 10^{12}$ bytes.

column1: What does a 1 Gbps network connection mean?
column2: It can download $1 \times 10^9$ bits per second (bits, not bytes).

column1: Order CPU, RAM and SSD from fastest to slowest.
column2: CPU (works in nanoseconds) > RAM (slower but still fast enough) > SSD (much slower than RAM).

column1: What happens when a program holds more data in memory than the RAM?
column2: The OS starts swapping/paging between RAM and SSD, the CPU frequently waits for data movement (I/O wait), and much less time is spent on actual computation.

column1: Case study I: at one 8-byte operation per cycle
column2: how long does a 2.5 GHz 64-bit CPU need to character-count 6000 articles of 200 bytes each?
column3: $6000 \times 200 = 1.2 \times 10^6$ bytes, so $1.2 \times 10^6 / (20 \times 10^9) = 6 \times 10^{-5}$ s, i.e. 0.006% of a second.

column1: In reality, what usually dominates runtime: arithmetic or data access?
column2: Data access: data must be fetched first (RAM latency ~100 ns, SSD latency in microseconds).

column1: Key message of case study I: where does the bottleneck move when data gets large?
column2: From CPU compute to network and storage I/O.

column1: How does fetching data over the network compare with reading it from local storage and memory?
column2: Getting the same amount of data from the network is much slower than processing it from your storage and memory.

column1: What is the key bottleneck consideration in case study II?
column2: I/O: moving data from SSD to memory burns out your CPU's time.

column1: When is it a good idea to go distributed, according to case study II?
column2: When your file is much larger than your memory.

column1: Case study III: the data grows from 4 GB to 200 GB on the same 8 GB machine. What goes wrong?
column2: The data no longer fits in RAM, so the machine keeps moving data between storage and memory and the CPU spends its time waiting instead of analysing; the computer stops responding.

column1: Name the four limits we hit as data grows on one computer.
column2: Storage limit, memory limit, time limit and reliability limit.

column1: What are the two situations in which distributed computing is needed?
column2: (1) You have big data to process (e.g. extract China-related news from 200 GB); (2) the data is not so big but the process is sophisticated (e.g. training a DNN with millions of parameters).

column1: In distributed computing, how are memory and machines organised?
column2: Each CPU has its own memory, and each machine is connected to the other machines across a network.

column1: In parallel computing, how is memory organised?
column2: In general, multiple CPUs share the same memory.

column1: Key challenge #1, partitioning: what questions must be answered?
column2: Split by rows, time, user or region? Are partitions balanced? Does one machine get much more work (data skew)?

column1: How do platforms handle partitioning?
column2: They break data into many small chunks and send the chunks to many machines (e.g. Hadoop MapReduce, Spark, BigQuery, Snowflake).

column1: Key challenge #2, communication overhead: what causes it?
column2: Moving data across the network, synchronizing intermediate results and coordinating task completion; too much of it can cancel the speed gains.

column1: How do platforms reduce communication overhead?
column2: They try to process data where it is stored and send only smaller summaries (e.g. MapReduce combine step, Spark keeping data in memory, smart query planning in cloud warehouses).

column1: Key challenge #3, fault tolerance: what mechanisms are needed?
column2: Detecting failed tasks, re-running lost work and recovering from partial progress, so the system continues even when some nodes fail.

column1: How do platforms provide fault tolerance?
column2: They detect the failure and automatically redo only the failed part.

column1: Key challenge #4, consistency & reproducibility: what are the risks in distributed runs?
column2: Different execution order, duplicate processing and missing late-arriving data.

column1: How do platforms ensure consistency and reproducibility?
column2: They run tasks in a controlled order, track progress and allow safe restart (e.g. Spark/MapReduce, Airflow/Prefect for scheduling, Kafka-based systems for continuous data).

column1: What are the four main components of a big data system?
column2: Common utilities, data storage, job scheduler and data processing.

column1: What is the major difference between Hadoop and Spark?
column2: How they use memory: Hadoop writes intermediate results to disk, whereas Spark keeps data in memory whenever possible, which makes it faster for many use cases.

column1: What are the benefits of a distributed big data framework?
column2: Larger-than-memory processing, faster runtime for large workloads and better reliability at scale.

column1: What are the costs of a distributed big data framework?
column2: More system complexity, more debugging difficulty and higher infrastructure/operation cost.

column1: What are the Five C's of data ethics?
column2: Consent, Clarity, Consistency, Control (and transparency) and Consequences (and harms).

column1: What does Consequences mean in the 5 Cs?
column2: Whether the data being collected could cause harm to an individual or a group.

column1: Name the four ethical concerns specific to distributed computing.
column2: Data privacy, data security, accountability and responsibility, and bias and fairness.

column1: Name the four (Gen)AI ethical challenges in the development and design stage.
column2: Bias and fairness; data source and permission; the "black box"; unequal resources and access.

column1: What is the "black box" problem?
column2: Big AI models are so complex that even their creators cannot fully explain their decisions, so it is hard to check, fix or challenge them.

column1: Name the six (Gen)AI ethical challenges in the usage stage.
column2: Privacy erosion and surveillance; accountability and liability; environmental impact; over-reliance and automation bias (trusting confident AI answers unchecked); intellectual property (cheating, plagiarism); malicious use.

column1: Name the four technical mitigations for AI ethics.
column2: Explainable AI (XAI), bias auditing, differential privacy and provenance tracking.

column1: What is differential privacy?
column2: A formal, mathematical framework that bounds how much results can change when one person's data is added or removed, limiting what can be learned about any single individual.

column1: What tools does provenance tracking use?
column2: "Model cards" and "datasheets for datasets", documenting the creation, use and limitations of models and data.

column1: Name the three governance and process mitigations for AI ethics.
column2: Ethics review boards (like an IRB for research), red teaming and clear lines of accountability.

column1: What is red teaming?
column2: Actively trying to "break" your system or find harmful uses of it before it is released.

column1: What are the two human-factor mitigations for AI ethics?
column2: Diverse teams (homogeneous teams miss blind spots) and ethics education (a core engineering requirement, not a soft skill).
